text: Gerald M. Friedman (1921–2011) was a distinguished professor in Geology and one of the founders of modern rock sedimentation. He held professorships at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, the Graduate Center of the City University of New York, and Brooklyn College. Born in Berlin, Germany, on July 27, 1921, Friedman, being Jewish, fled the Nazis in 1938 and settled in England. He earned a bachelor's degree from the University of London in 1945, majoring in chemistry and minoring in geology. In 1945, he immigrated to the United States and worked as a Chemist for three years at Squibb. Friedman authored 573 papers and 19 books, including the highly cited work "Principles of Sedimentology." He received several awards, such as the William H. Twenhofel Medal in 1997, the Sidney Powers Memorial Award in 2000, and the Mary C. Rabbitt History And Philosophy of Geology Award in 2005. Friedman founded and directed the Northeastern Science Foundation, which organizes symposia and publishes journals such as Northeastern Geology, Environmental Science, Carbonates and Evaporites, and the Carbonates and Evaporites journal. The Sue Tyler Friedman Medal, named in honor of his wife, Sue (Tyler) Friedman, was established in recognition of her contribution.
